title: 2-Link Planar Arm Forward Kinematics (theta_1, theta_2 -> x, y)

blocks.x: Add a second link ($L_2$) and an elbow motor ($\theta_2$) to your planar robot arm, relate the **relative joint angle** $\theta_2$ to the forearm's **absolute world angle** ($\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$), and compute the **end-effector** (hand) position $(x, y)$ by chaining two tip-to-tail vectors in Python.

items.x: **New ideas (max 2):**

**Absolute link angle ($\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$) from relative elbow joint angle $\theta_2$**: Because the elbow motor is bolted to the end of Link 1, turning the shoulder by $\theta_1$ rotates the forearm too—so the forearm's angle relative to the world $+x$ axis is $\theta_1 + \theta_2$.

**Chaining tip-to-tail vectors for 2-link forward kinematics**: Adding the upper-arm vector $(L_1 \cos\theta_1, L_1 \sin\theta_1)$ and the forearm vector $(L_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2), L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2))$ to locate both the elbow and the **end-effector** tip $(x, y)$.
**New syntax:** None (`math.cos`, `math.sin`, `math.radians` from Track P).
**Target time (unmeasured — [log yours](../.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/beginner-timing-log.md)):** Typical: 1.5–2.0 hours | Slow-learner: 2.5–3.5 hours

blocks.x: Idea 1: Absolute link angle ($\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$) from relative elbow joint angle $\theta_2$

items.x: **Primary resource:** [Math is Fun — Angles](https://www.mathsisfun.com/angles.html) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Names of Angles`** and **`Positive and Negative Angles`** (`+CCW` vs. `-CW`).
**What to skip:** Skip reflex angle naming quizzes.

**Key takeaway:** On a real 2-link robot arm, the elbow encoder measures the **relative joint angle** $\theta_2$—how much the forearm bends relative to the straight line of Link 1 ($\theta_2 = 0^\circ$ means the elbow is completely straight!). Because Link 1 is already tilted at angle $\theta_1$ relative to the world $+x$ axis, the forearm's **absolute angle** relative to the world $+x$ axis is the sum of both angles: $\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$.

blocks.x: Idea 2: Chaining tip-to-tail vectors for 2-link forward kinematics

items.x: **Primary resource:** [Math is Fun — Vectors ("Adding Vectors")](https://www.mathsisfun.com/algebra/vectors.html) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Vectors`**, **`Notation`**, and **`Adding Vectors`** (adding the $x$-components together and adding the $y$-components together).
**What to skip:** Skip vector multiplication (dot and cross products).
**Key takeaway:** A 2-link arm is simply two 1-link vectors chained **tip-to-tail**:
**Shoulder to Elbow (`Link 1`, length $L_1$, world angle $\theta_1$):** $x_{\text{elbow}} = L_1 \cos(\theta_1)$ and $y_{\text{elbow}} = L_1 \sin(\theta_1)$.
**Elbow to End-Effector (`Link 2`, length $L_2$, world angle $\theta_1 + \theta_2$):** $\Delta x_2 = L_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$ and $\Delta y_2 = L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$.
**Total End-Effector (hand/gripper tip) position $(x, y)$:** $x = L_1 \cos(\theta_1) + L_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$ and $y = L_1 \sin(\theta_1) + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$.

blocks.x: In **2-link forward kinematics**, we find the **end-effector** position $(x, y)$ by **chaining tip-to-tail vectors**: first the upper-arm vector $(L_1 \cos\theta_1, L_1 \sin\theta_1)$ from the shoulder `(0, 0)` to the elbow $(x_1, y_1)$, and then the forearm vector $(L_2 \cos\theta_{12}, L_2 \sin\theta_{12})$ from the elbow to the hand.

Why is the angle inside the second cosine and sine the **absolute link angle** $\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$ instead of just the **relative joint angle** $\theta_2$?
Test it with an extreme-case sanity check (`Lesson 00.3`)! Suppose $L_1 = 0.15\text{ m}$ and $L_2 = 0.15\text{ m}$. Keep the elbow locked completely straight ($\theta_2 = 0^\circ$) and raise the shoulder straight up to $\theta_1 = +90^\circ$:

items.x: With the **correct** formula $\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90^\circ + 0^\circ = 90^\circ$, both links point straight up along $+y$, giving $(x, y) = (0.00\text{ m}, +0.30\text{ m})$.
If you **forgot** to add $\theta_1$ and wrote $L_2 \cos(\theta_2) = L_2 \cos(0^\circ)$, your code would claim the forearm always points horizontally right regardless of how the shoulder moves!
**What is simulated and in which tool:**

**In Python 3:** Complete `fk_2link` (`TODO 1` and `TODO 2`) to compute both the elbow position $(x_1, y_1)$ and the **end-effector** tip position $(x, y)$ for a 2-link planar arm ($L_1 = 0.15\text{ m}$, $L_2 = 0.15\text{ m}$) across 4 test postures.
**What is real-hardware only:** Physical link self-collision when the forearm folds past $\pm 150^\circ$ and hits the upper arm bracket.

import math

# The two links every posture is drawn with. Drag either one and the printed tip follows.
L1_M = 0.15  # @slider 0.05 0.40 0.01
L2_M = 0.15  # @slider 0.05 0.40 0.01


def fk_2link(l1_m, l2_m, theta1_deg, theta2_deg):
    # TODO 1: Convert theta1_deg and theta2_deg to radians (t1, t2) and compute
    #         the absolute forearm angle t12 = t1 + t2
    t1 = 0.0
    t12 = 0.0

    # TODO 2: Compute elbow coordinates (x1, y1) and end-effector tip coordinates (x, y)
    x1 = 0.0
    y1 = 0.0
    x = 0.0
    y = 0.0
    return x1, y1, x, y


postures = [
    ("Straight Right", 0.0, 0.0),
    ("L-Bend Up     ", 0.0, 90.0),
    ("Straight Up   ", 90.0, 0.0),
    ("Reach Diagonal", 30.0, 60.0),
]

for label, q1_deg, q2_deg in postures:
    ex, ey, tx, ty = fk_2link(L1_M, L2_M, q1_deg, q2_deg)
    print(f"{label} (q1={q1_deg:4.0f}, q2={q2_deg:4.0f}) -> elbow=({ex:+.3f}, {ey:+.3f}) m | tip=({tx:+.3f}, {ty:+.3f}) m")

def fk_2link(l1_m, l2_m, theta1_deg, theta2_deg):
    t1 = math.radians(theta1_deg)
    t2 = math.radians(theta2_deg)
    t12 = t1 + t2
    x1 = l1_m * math.cos(t1)
    y1 = l1_m * math.sin(t1)
    x = x1 + l2_m * math.cos(t12)
    y = y1 + l2_m * math.sin(t12)
    return x1, y1, x, y

import math


def fk_2link(l1_m, l2_m, theta1_deg, theta2_deg):
    t1 = math.radians(theta1_deg)
    t2 = math.radians(theta2_deg)
    t12 = t1 + t2
    x1 = l1_m * math.cos(t1)
    y1 = l1_m * math.sin(t1)
    x = x1 + l2_m * math.cos(t12)
    y = y1 + l2_m * math.sin(t12)
    return x1, y1, x, y


postures = [
    ("Straight Right", 0.0, 0.0),
    ("L-Bend Up     ", 0.0, 90.0),
    ("Straight Up   ", 90.0, 0.0),
    ("Reach Diagonal", 30.0, 60.0),
]

for label, q1_deg, q2_deg in postures:
    ex, ey, tx, ty = fk_2link(0.15, 0.15, q1_deg, q2_deg)
    print(f"{label} (q1={q1_deg:4.0f}, q2={q2_deg:4.0f}) -> elbow=({ex:+.3f}, {ey:+.3f}) m | tip=({tx:+.3f}, {ty:+.3f}) m")

items.x: **Writing `l2_m * math.cos(t2)` instead of `l2_m * math.cos(t1 + t2)`:** The elbow angle $\theta_2$ is measured relative to Link 1, so its angle relative to the horizontal $+x$ world axis is always $\theta_1 + \theta_2$.
**Converting $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ to radians *after* adding a radian and a degree:** Never mix radians and degrees in `t1 + t2`; convert both to radians first!

**Tracing `Reach Diagonal` ($\theta_1 = 30^\circ, \theta_2 = 60^\circ$):** Why does the end-effector tip in the 4th test case (`q1 = 30 deg, q2 = 60 deg`) have the exact same $x$-coordinate (`+0.130 m`) as the elbow? Answer

blocks.x: Because the forearm's absolute world angle is $\theta_{12} = 30^\circ + 60^\circ = \mathbf{90^\circ}$ (pointing straight up along $+y$!), so Link 2 adds $\Delta x_2 = L_2 \cos(90^\circ) = 0.000\text{ m}$ horizontally and $+0.150\text{ m}$ vertically!

items.x: **Minimum and maximum reach of a 2-link arm:** If $L_1 = 0.20\text{ m}$ and $L_2 = 0.12\text{ m}$, what is the farthest distance $r_{\max}$ from `(0, 0)` the end-effector can reach ($\theta_2 = 0^\circ$), and what is the closest distance $r_{\min}$ when folded completely back ($\theta_2 = 180^\circ$)? Answer
Maximum reach: $r_{\max} = L_1 + L_2 = 0.20 + 0.12 = \mathbf{0.32\text{ m}}$.
Minimum reach: $r_{\min} = \lvert L_1 - L_2 \rvert = 0.20 - 0.12 = \mathbf{0.08\text{ m}}$.
The elbow motor measures a **relative joint angle** $\theta_2$, so the forearm's absolute world angle is $\theta_{12} = \theta_1 + \theta_2$.

**2-link forward kinematics** chains both link vectors tip-to-tail to locate the **end-effector**: $x = L_1 \cos\theta_1 + L_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$ and $y = L_1 \sin\theta_1 + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$.
